title: The Modi government’s capitulation on Agnipath cannot undo the damage it has done
image_caption: First batch of youth recruited under the Agnipath scheme undergo physical training.ANI Photo
content_html:
On 4 November, the Narendra Modi government beat a significant retreat on Agnipath, the military recruitment scheme it had introduced four years ago in the face of opposition from the defence services. The scheme allowed for youth to be inducted into the armed forces on a contractual basis rather than a long-term enlistment. The retreat came days before three quarters of the first cohort of Agniveers—the soldiers contracted under the scheme—were due to be released. Under the new arrangement, the 75 percent of Agniveers not selected for retention after their initial four-year term will be offered a two-year “second tour of duty.” After those extra two years, willing personnel meeting selection criteria can enrol as regular soldiers. The original 25 percent retention on merit remains, but the practical effect is a pathway toward near-full absorption for those who want it. (Subsequent media reports have added further confusion by suggesting that the revisions will apply only to those currently serving as Agniveers, and that no decision has been taken about the incoming cohorts of contractual soldiers.)

Announcing this climbdown, the chief of defence staff, NS Raja Subramani, insisted the Agnipath scheme “has not been discontinued,” but this was little more than face-saving. After all, the scheme’s defining feature was the deliberate creation of a large cohort of contractual soldiers who would exit service after four years with a cash package and no pension, no ex-serviceman status and limited prospects in civilian life. The official release attributes the U-turn to outstanding performance, positive feedback and the alignment of recruits’ aspirations with organisational efficiency. It lists fitness, motivation, technological adaptability and recruitment improvements as achievements, then declares that Agnipath will continue. But those realisations do not explain why the original four-year exit arrangement is now being substantially altered. This is nothing but an attempt at political survival and short-term management of political discontent. As has been the norm with Modi since 2014, political panic has forced a tactical retreat, while official claims try to spin the narrative surrounding it. The timing of upcoming elections in Punjab, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh is obvious.

Introduced in June 2022, after a recruitment freeze that lasted two years, Agnipath was billed as a revolutionary modernisation project that would slash the crippling defence pension bill, lower the average age of the armed forces, get more tech-savvy soldiers and infuse the citizenry with neo-nationalist discipline. Though never formally acknowledged, the main driver was fiscal. A study found that an Agniveer cost the government almost a quarter less than an average soldier. Over a period of two decades, with Agniveers expected to make up a majority of the forces, the savings would be substantial.

Having invested politically in One Rank One Pension, Modi found it difficult to mount an open assault on existing pension entitlements. Short-term recruitment offered another route to reduce future obligations by changing the terms for future soldiers. The chief of the army staff at the time, General MM Naravane, resisted a full rollout and preferred a limited pilot project but was overruled by the prime minister’s office. The scheme was imposed against the wishes of the service chiefs, and anyone who dared criticise it, whether a veteran admiral or a school-leaving aspirant, was demonised by pro-establishment voices in the media.

title: The ethnic histories of Ram and Krishna
content_html:
ALTHOUGH THE IDEA of the avatar does not appear in Vedic literature, there is a belief within Hinduism that there are ten incarnations of Vishnu. The first nine of these have appeared and Kalki, the final avatar, is expected at the end of Kaliyuga. The Ram and Krishna avatars of Vishnu are the most prominent because of the popularity of the Ramayana and Mahabharata. The Ramayana is the story of the legendary prince of Kosala and expounds Ram’s exile and his march towards Kishkinda to capture vanars, and later towards Lanka to seize Ravan. Eventually, Ram is coronated as king of Ayodhya to inaugurate the ideal form of state: Ram Rajya. The Mahabharata is the story of a war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas, two groups of cousins, in which Krishna is presented as a canny strategist. He is a war hero, a counsellor to the Pandavas. His origin stories came later.

While Ram and Krishna are both avatars of the same deity, they come from different lineages and, I argue, represent contrasting ideologies. The Sangh Parivar has tended to be territorial about the figure of Ram, while Krishna is claimed most significantly by the Yadav community. Since the 1980s, Ram has been aggressively used as political currency by the Hindu Right to gain electoral power. For Yadavs, Krishna is a cultural hero who represents productive labour.

The Sangh Parivar baulks at the very fact that there are different versions of the Ramayana in existence. In 2011, Delhi University was forced to remove AK Ramanujan’s celebrated essay “Three Hundred Ramayanas” after a writ petition was filed in court claiming the essay “hurt religious sentiments.” Ramanujan wrote that he preferred the word “tellings” to “versions or variants” because the “latter terms can and typically do imply that there is an invariant, an original or Ur-text—usually Valmiki’s Sanskrit Ramayana, the earliest and most prestigious of them all.” But, he argued, “it is not always Valmiki's narrative that is carried from one language to another.”

More and more, alternate readings of the Ramayana have been subordinated to a singular mythological reading that seeks to preserve the dominance of Brahminical Hinduism. This Ramayana spreads the glory of Ram’s monogamy (ekapatni), strict patriarchy (pitru vakya paripalan), varna dharma (eka dharma) and, of course, one arrow (eka baan), and symbolises how the plural culture of India has been swallowed by the rigid and monotonous value system of the Aryans. The Ramayana ends with his salvation and the distribution of the kingdom to his offspring, but there is no mention of his grandsons or great-grandsons. On the other hand, the Mahabharata carries details about Krishna’s genealogy, alluding to his grandfather Ugrasena and to his grandson Anirudh.

title: The inability to address Delhi’s air crisis is a sign of a failing democracy
image_caption: A man crosses a pedestrian bridge amid another season of smog in Delhi. For the middle class, in the Modi years, cultural boosterism and ethnonationalism have taken precedence over physical and economic well-being.Adnan Abidi / Reuters
content_html:
As winter descended, and Delhi embarked on what has become its regular season of poisonous air—a malaise exacerbated by open violations of the ban on firecrackers during Diwali—sections of the press and the liberal elite enacted their annual ritual of outrage and helplessness. Environmentalists lamented the government’s fitful and ineffective action; pulmonologists saw their wards filling up; citizens of the national capital wheezed and choked as the Air Quality Index shot up to hazardous levels.

The air crisis in Delhi, and large parts of north India, has come to be framed predominantly as a failure of environmental and public-health management. The intriguing puzzle, though, is not the repetitive nature of the crisis but the collective inability to fix—or even substantially mitigate—the problem. This is yet another sign of India’s failing democracy.

In March 2021, Freedom House, a US think tank that evaluates democracies across the world, downgraded India’s status from “free” to “partly free” in its annual report. “Political rights and civil liberties in the country have deteriorated since Narendra Modi became prime minister in 2014, with increased pressure on human rights organizations, rising intimidation of academics and journalists, and a spate of bigoted attacks, including lynchings, aimed at Muslims,” the report noted. “Under Modi, India appears to have abandoned its potential to serve as a global democratic leader, elevating narrow Hindu nationalist interests at the expense of its founding values of inclusion and equal rights for all.” That same month, the V-Dem Institute, an independent research organisation based in Sweden, also reclassified India, observing that “the world’s largest democracy has turned into an electoral autocracy.” Many other global monitors have arrived at a similar conclusion. The Economist Intelligence Unit—a sister organisation of The Economist, which once pinned great hope on Modi as a free-market reformer—has bracketed India as a “flawed democracy.”

While such reports accurately summarise Modi’s assault on democratic institutions, minority rights and free expression, lesser attention is usually given to the decline of routine accountability as one of the consequences of India’s democratic backsliding. In failing democracies, even pressing subjects of all-encompassing import such as the air crisis are unable to become the focus of public conversation and thus unable to be addressed.
